practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of an abiotic component of an ecosystem?
A) Decomposer fungi
B) Soil moisture
C) Earthworms
D) Algae
practice_questions.marks: B) Soil moisture [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two biomes found at high latitudes.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each, max 2:
• Polar / tundra
• Boreal / coniferous forest
• Temperate forest (in higher mid-latitudes)
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which abiotic and biotic components of an ecosystem are interdependent.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per developed point, max 4:
• Soil supplies plants with water and nutrients (1) which support animals further up the food chain (2 — developed).
• Decomposer bacteria and fungi break down dead matter (1) returning nutrients to the soil for new plant growth (2 — developed).
• Climate (rainfall, temperature) determines vegetation type (1) which in turn determines the animal communities present (2 — developed).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe and explain why tropical rainforests cluster around the equator.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies equator latitude (0-10°N/S). Explains the global atmospheric circulation: rising warm air at the Equator (Hadley cell) cools and produces heavy convectional rainfall almost daily. Combination of constant warmth (25-28°C) and 2000+ mm rainfall sustains rainforest. Names major locations (Amazon, Congo Basin, South East Asia).
Secure: Identifies climate plus location with one cause.
Developing: Names rainforest locations without explaining climate cause.
Emerging: Generic; no causes.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the global circulation of the atmosphere produces the pattern of biomes from the equator to the tropics.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains rising air at the equator producing tropical rainforests; descending air at 20-30°N/S producing hot deserts; rising air at temperate latitudes producing forests; descending polar air producing tundra. Uses named biomes (Sahara at 20-30°N, Amazon at the Equator). Connects atmosphere to climate to vegetation to animal communities. Acknowledges the role of ocean currents in modifying coastal climates.
Secure: Two zones explained with named biomes.
Developing: One zone explained.
Emerging: Names biomes without atmospheric mechanism.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
“Climate is the most important factor determining the location of the world's biomes.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• discuss the role of climate
• discuss other factors (ocean currents, soil, altitude, human activity)
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument. Climate — latitude controls temperature and rainfall, producing predictable biome belts (Amazon equatorial rainforest, Sahara at 20-30°N). Other factors — ocean currents shift coastal climates (the Gulf Stream gives the UK temperate forest at 50°N when continental Russia at the same latitude is taiga); altitude creates vertical biome zones (rainforest to alpine tundra in the Andes); human activity has cleared about a third of the original global forest cover for farmland. Conclusion explicitly weighs whether climate is dominant or merely the framework that other factors modify.
Secure: Both sides with named examples; conclusion follows the argument.
Developing: One-sided; conclusion present but weak.
Emerging: Generic; no examples; no clear judgement.
[8 marks plus 3 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of mechanical weathering in a UK upland landscape?
A) Acid rain dissolving limestone
B) Tree roots widening a crack in a slab of granite
C) Freeze-thaw shattering rock on a Lake District peak
D) A river depositing sand on its floodplain
practice_questions.marks: C) Freeze-thaw shattering rock on a Lake District peak [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two characteristics that make UK upland landscapes different from UK lowland landscapes.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each, max 2:
• Higher elevation / steeper slopes
• Harder, more resistant rocks (e.g. granite, slate)
• Cooler, wetter climate
• Thinner, more acidic soils
• Sparser settlement / sheep grazing rather than arable farming
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which freeze-thaw weathering shapes upland UK landscapes.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per developed point, max 4:
• Water enters cracks in exposed rock at the surface (1) and freezes overnight, expanding by about 9% to widen the crack (2 — developed).
• Repeated cycles cause angular fragments to break off (1) which collect at the foot of the slope as scree (2 — developed).
• Freeze-thaw is most active where temperatures cross 0°C frequently (1), giving sharp peaks and shattered surfaces in places like Snowdonia (2 — developed).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe and explain the difference between weathering and erosion, using examples from the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear definitions of both processes with explicit contrast (in situ versus involving transport), supported by accurate UK examples (e.g. limestone weathering at Malham Cove versus river abrasion in the Pennines).
Secure: Both processes defined with at least one UK example each; some explanation of difference.
Developing: Definitions present but examples generic or partial; weathering and erosion may be partly conflated.
Emerging: Simple definitions with little distinction; examples missing or inaccurate.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how mass movement and erosion work together to reshape UK slopes. Refer to specific UK examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains the cause-effect chain — weathering loosens rock, gravity drives mass movement, erosion attacks the slope foot — using UK examples (e.g. Holderness slumping on saturated clay; freeze-thaw and rockfall in Cumbria). Connects processes rather than treating them separately.
Secure: Explains both processes with a UK example each and shows how they interact.
Developing: Names processes and gives one example, but interaction is implicit or limited.
Emerging: Lists processes without explanation or examples; processes treated as isolated.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
“Geology is the most important factor shaping UK landscapes.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• explain how geology shapes UK landscapes
• consider the role of climate and human activity
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A balanced evaluation. Geology explains rock resistance, soil type and slope steepness (e.g. granite uplands of Dartmoor versus chalk lowlands of the Downs). Climate drives geomorphic processes — freeze-thaw in cold uplands, chemical weathering of limestone, water erosion of saturated lowlands. Human activity (deforestation, farming, urbanisation, flood defences) modifies all of these. A justified conclusion explicitly weighs the three.
Secure: Considers two or three factors with UK evidence and a clear conclusion that follows the argument.
Developing: Discusses geology with limited reference to climate or human activity; conclusion present but weakly justified.
Emerging: One-sided argument; few examples; no clear judgement.
[8 marks plus 3 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following landforms is most likely to be found in the upper course of a UK river?
A) A floodplain
B) An ox-bow lake
C) A waterfall
D) A delta
practice_questions.marks: C) A waterfall [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two landforms produced by lateral erosion.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each, max 2:
• Meander
• Ox-bow lake
• River cliff (outer bend)
• Slip-off slope (inner bend)
• Wide valley floor
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a waterfall retreats over time.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per developed point, max 4:
• Hydraulic action and abrasion erode the soft rock under the lip (1) creating a plunge pool below the waterfall (2 — developed).
• The undercut overhang of resistant rock collapses (1) causing the waterfall to step back upstream and leaving a gorge of recession (2 — developed).
• High Force on the River Tees has retreated about 700 m along the Whin Sill (1), leaving the gorge below the falls (2 — developed).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe and explain how a meander develops in the middle course of a river.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Faster water on the outside of the bend erodes a river cliff through hydraulic action and abrasion; slower water on the inside deposits a slip-off slope. Continuous lateral erosion exaggerates the curve over time. UK example used (e.g. Tees near Yarm).
Secure: Both processes described with location of erosion versus deposition; UK example referenced.
Developing: Erosion described but deposition partial; example generic.
Emerging: Description of meander shape only; processes implicit.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how human activity has changed the geomorphic processes operating in your chosen UK river basin.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Uses a named UK basin (e.g. the Tees) with specific examples — reservoirs at Cow Green starve the lower river of sediment; the Tees Barrage controls tidal flow; meander straightening at Stockton accelerated flow and increased downstream flood risk; floodplain reconnection at Saltholme reverses this. Each example links a human action to a measurable change in a geomorphic process.
Secure: Two or three named human interventions linked to process changes.
Developing: Lists human activities without clear links to geomorphic processes.
Emerging: Generic comments about pollution or building; no specific case study evidence.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
“Geology is more important than human activity in shaping UK river landscapes.”
Evaluate this statement using your case study.
In your answer you should:
• explain how geology shapes landforms
• explain how human activity shapes landforms
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both arguments developed with case-study evidence. Geology controls long-term form — the Whin Sill creates High Force, soft rocks below allow the gorge of recession, lowland clays support floodplains. Human activity reshapes process rates — reservoirs reduce sediment supply, the Tees Barrage controls tidal flow, straightening alters flood risk. Conclusion explicitly weighs the two and justifies a judgement (e.g. geology sets the framework, but at human timescales activity is the dominant change agent).
Secure: Both factors discussed with case study evidence; conclusion stated clearly.
Developing: One factor dominant; conclusion present but weakly supported.
Emerging: Generic comments; little case study evidence; no clear judgement.
[8 marks plus 3 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the world's largest tropical rainforest?
A) Madagascan
B) Congo Basin
C) Amazon
D) Australasian
practice_questions.marks: C) Amazon [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two threats to the Amazon rainforest.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each, max 2:
• Deforestation for cattle ranching
• Deforestation for soya farming
• Illegal logging
• Gold mining
• Climate-change driven drought and forest fires
• Road building
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the rainforest nutrient cycle.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per developed point, max 4:
• Most nutrients are stored in the biomass (1) rather than in the soil, which is thin and acidic (2 — developed).
• Decomposition is rapid (1) because warm wet conditions accelerate fungi, bacteria and termite activity (2 — developed).
• Released nutrients are taken up immediately by tree roots (1) before they can wash away in heavy rainfall (2 — developed).
• If trees are cleared, the nutrient store is lost (1) and the soil cannot support farming for long (2 — developed).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe and explain how the Amazon rainforest is valuable to humans.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies multiple values with statistics. Local — supports 30 million people including 350+ indigenous groups; supplies timber, rubber, Brazil nuts, acai. Regional — stabilises rainfall across South America. Global — stores 100 billion tonnes of carbon, provides 6% of the world's oxygen, source of medicines (quinine, curare). Connects each value to the rainforest process that delivers it.
Secure: Three values with at least one statistic.
Developing: Two values with limited specifics.
Emerging: Generic comments about ‘biodiversity’.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how sustainable management strategies aim to protect the Amazon.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies multiple strategies with specific examples. Indigenous land rights — managed indigenous land has lower deforestation than government-protected zones. Selective logging takes few trees per hectare, leaving canopy intact. Ecotourism — Mamiraua Sustainable Reserve in Brazil generates revenue without clearance. International payments — REDD+ pays countries to keep forests standing. Tightened Brazilian enforcement from 2023 has cut deforestation sharply. Acknowledges trade-offs (development vs protection) and the tipping point at 20-25%.
Secure: Three strategies with named examples.
Developing: Two strategies; effects partial.
Emerging: Generic; few facts.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
“The international community is doing enough to protect the world's tropical rainforests.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• discuss successful international actions
• discuss limitations and continuing threats
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument. Successes — REDD+ payments, EU Deforestation Regulation, slowing of Brazilian deforestation since 2023, indigenous land protection, certification schemes (FSC). Limitations — 17% of Amazon already cleared, tipping point at 20-25% looming, illegal logging continues, climate change accelerates drought and fire, demand for soya and beef in rich countries drives clearance. Conclusion explicitly weighs progress against scale of threat. Specific Amazon and global statistics throughout.
Secure: Both sides considered with named examples; conclusion follows the argument.
Developing: One-sided; conclusion present but weak.
Emerging: Generic; few facts; no clear judgement.
[8 marks plus 3 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following landforms is created by deposition?
A) Stack
B) Headland
C) Spit
D) Wave-cut platform
practice_questions.marks: C) Spit [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two characteristics of destructive waves.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each, max 2:
• Tall / steep wave height
• Strong backwash
• High frequency / many per minute
• Carry sediment away from the beach
• Associated with storm conditions
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a stack is formed from a headland.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per developed point, max 4:
• Hydraulic action enlarges a crack in the headland (1) into a cave (2 — developed).
• Continued erosion forces the cave through the headland (1) creating an arch (2 — developed).
• Weathering and erosion weaken the arch roof (1) which collapses to leave a stack of resistant rock (2 — developed).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe and explain how longshore drift moves sediment along the UK coast.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Waves approach the coast at an angle (often driven by prevailing wind). Swash carries sediment up the beach at the same angle; backwash returns sediment straight down the beach under gravity. Sediment progresses along the coast in a zig-zag pattern. UK example used (e.g. Holderness to Spurn Head).
Secure: Process described with both swash and backwash; UK example referenced.
Developing: Process partial; example missing or generic.
Emerging: Description of waves only without zig-zag mechanism.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how geology and human activity together influence erosion at your chosen UK coast case study.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Uses Holderness or another named UK coast. Geology — boulder clay is unconsolidated and slumps when saturated; underlying chalk at Flamborough Head resists erosion forming the iconic stacks. Human activity — sea defences at Hornsea and Mappleton block longshore drift south, starving Easington of sediment and accelerating erosion. Connects geology and human action through specific evidence.
Secure: Both factors with one named example each; clear linkage.
Developing: One factor with case study; the other implicit.
Emerging: Generic statements about cliffs eroding; no case study facts.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
“Hard engineering should always be used to protect UK coasts from erosion.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• discuss benefits of hard engineering
• discuss drawbacks and alternatives
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument. Benefits — sea walls and groynes protect homes and infrastructure; rip-rap dissipates wave energy; defended villages like Hornsea remain viable. Drawbacks — high cost, visual impact, and crucially the sediment-starvation effect that accelerates erosion further along the coast (Easington). Alternatives — soft engineering at Medmerry created salt marsh and protected inland villages more sustainably; managed retreat acknowledges that protecting every metre of coastline is unaffordable. Conclusion explicitly weighs cost, sustainability and equity between defended and undefended coasts.
Secure: Both sides considered with at least one named UK example each; conclusion follows the argument.
Developing: One side dominant; conclusion present but weakly justified.
Emerging: Generic answer; little UK evidence; no clear judgement.
[8 marks plus 3 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the world's largest coral reef?
A) Florida Reef
B) Andros Coral Reef
C) Great Barrier Reef
D) Red Sea Coral Reef
practice_questions.marks: C) Great Barrier Reef [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two conditions a coral reef needs to grow.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each, max 2:
• Warm water (23-29°C)
• Salty water
• Plenty of sunlight
• Clear, low-nutrient water
• Shallow depth (less than 50 m)
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two effects of mass bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per developed point, max 4:
• Coral polyps expel zooxanthellae algae (1) and turn white as their colour is lost (2 — developed).
• Coral starvation if conditions don't recover (1) leading to large-scale coral death (2 — developed).
• Loss of habitat for thousands of fish, mollusc and turtle species (1) cascading through the food web (2 — developed).
• Tourism revenue affected (1) with parts of the reef closed to visitors after the 2024 event (2 — developed).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe and explain how the symbiotic relationship between coral and algae underpins reef ecosystems.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies symbiosis as a close mutually beneficial relationship. Explains both directions: zooxanthellae algae photosynthesise and share sugars and oxygen with coral; coral provides shelter and access to sunlight. Connects this to the productivity that supports 25% of marine species. Acknowledges that disrupting the relationship (through warming, pollution) causes the whole reef to collapse.
Secure: Symbiosis defined with both partners' contributions; some reef ecosystem context.
Developing: One side of the relationship explained.
Emerging: Names symbiosis without mechanism.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how human activity threatens the Great Barrier Reef.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies multiple human-driven threats with statistics. Climate change — sea-surface temperatures 1-2°C above normal trigger mass bleaching; five events between 2016 and 2024, 75% of the reef affected in 2024. Water pollution — sediment from sugar cane farming, fertiliser run-off feeding crown-of-thorns starfish outbreaks. Coastal development — ports and dredging damage reef edges. Connects local pressures to the dominant global driver of climate change.
Secure: Three threats with named examples.
Developing: Two threats with partial explanation.
Emerging: Generic; no statistics.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
“The Great Barrier Reef can be saved through local management strategies.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• discuss what local management can achieve
• discuss the role of global climate action
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument. Local management — Marine Protected Areas (344,000 km<sup>2</sup>; 33% no-take), water quality improvements, crown-of-thorns culls, coral gardening, Reef 2050 Plan funding. Climate action — even with perfect local management, scientists project a 70-90% loss of coral reefs worldwide even at 1.5°C of warming. Global emissions cuts are essential. Conclusion explicitly weighs whether local management buys time without solving the underlying problem.
Secure: Both sides considered with named examples; conclusion follows the argument.
Developing: One-sided; conclusion present but weak.
Emerging: Generic; few facts; no clear judgement.
[8 marks plus 3 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the UK's largest single export market?
A) China
B) Germany
C) Ireland
D) The United States
practice_questions.marks: D) The United States [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two examples of UK soft power.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each, max 2:
• English language
• BBC World Service
• Premier League / Football
• UK universities (Oxford, Cambridge, Imperial)
• British music / film / fashion industries
• The Royal Family
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways the UK is connected to the wider world.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per developed point, max 4:
• Trade in goods and services (1) — e.g. car exports to the EU and pharmaceutical exports to the USA (2 — developed).
• Migration flows (1) — record net migration of 944,000 in the year to March 2023, including EU workers, Commonwealth professionals and refugees from Ukraine and Hong Kong (2 — developed).
• Cultural exports (1) — the BBC reaches 365 million people weekly and Premier League matches are watched in over 200 countries (2 — developed).
• Political alliances (1) — UN Security Council membership, NATO, G7 and the Commonwealth of 56 countries (2 — developed).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe and explain how the UK's trading patterns reflect its position as a high-skill economy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies that the UK exports high-value services (finance, legal, consultancy) and high-skill manufactured goods (cars, pharmaceuticals, aerospace) while importing manufactured consumer goods (Chinese electronics, Bangladeshi clothing) and raw materials (Norwegian gas). Explains that this reflects comparative advantage in skills and knowledge.
Secure: Clear export/import contrast with named goods; explanation of high-skill specialisation.
Developing: Trade pattern described but explanation thin or generic.
Emerging: Lists trading partners; no analysis.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how membership of international organisations strengthens the UK's global influence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Uses specific organisations (UN Security Council permanent seat, NATO, G7, Commonwealth, World Trade Organization) to show how each delivers distinct influence — security alliances, economic coordination, trade rules, post-colonial soft power. Links membership to outcomes (e.g. UK aid programme, military operations, trade negotiations).
Secure: Multiple organisations named with linkage to specific UK influence.
Developing: Names organisations but limited link to influence.
Emerging: Lists organisations without explanation.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
“The UK benefits more than it loses from being globally connected.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• discuss benefits of global connections
• discuss costs and vulnerabilities
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced evaluation. Benefits — access to global markets (40% of exports to EU), services exports (London as financial hub), cultural soft power (Premier League in 200+ countries), labour from migration, food and energy imports. Costs — vulnerability to supply chain shocks (2021 shipping crisis), dependence on imported energy and food, exposure to global financial volatility, political tensions over migration, environmental footprint of long supply chains. Conclusion explicitly weighs the two and offers a justified judgement.
Secure: Both sides considered with named UK examples; conclusion follows the argument.
Developing: One-sided argument; conclusion present but weak.
Emerging: Generic; few facts; no clear judgement.
[8 marks plus 3 SPaG]

before.exam_tip_html: Be specific in 6-mark answers about UK trade. Examiners reward named partners (USA, Germany, Netherlands), named goods (Scotch, cars, pharmaceuticals) and current statistics (40% of exports to EU, 46% of food imported). For 8-mark evaluations, weigh the benefits of being globally connected (markets, soft power) against the vulnerabilities (supply chain shocks, energy dependence) before reaching a justified conclusion.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a Low-Income Developing Country (LIDC)?
A) United States
B) China
C) Mozambique
D) Brazil
practice_questions.marks: C) Mozambique [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two indicators used to measure development.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each, max 2:
• GNI per capita
• Human Development Index (HDI)
• Internet users per 100 people
• Life expectancy
• Literacy rate / years of schooling
• Infant mortality rate
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two advantages of using the Human Development Index over GNI per capita.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per developed point, max 4:
• HDI combines income, life expectancy and schooling (1) giving a more rounded picture of development than money alone (2 — developed).
• HDI captures social progress (1) so a country with high income but low life expectancy or poor schooling scores lower (2 — developed).
• HDI is internationally comparable (1) and updated regularly by the UN (2 — developed).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe and explain how Advanced Countries (ACs), Emerging and Developing Countries (EDCs) and Low-Income Developing Countries (LIDCs) differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Defines all three categories with named examples. ACs — high incomes, high HDI, mature service economies (USA, Japan, UK). EDCs — rising incomes, expanding manufacturing, fast-growing cities (China, India, Brazil). LIDCs — low incomes, agriculture-based, weak infrastructure (Ethiopia, Mozambique, Bangladesh). Uses statistics (HDI scores, GNI figures) to support each.
Secure: Three categories with named examples and clear distinctions.
Developing: Two categories explained.
Emerging: Lists categories without distinction.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why no single development indicator gives a complete picture of a country's development.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Multiple indicators discussed with limitations. GNI per capita — ignores inequality, informal economies and quality of life. HDI — updates slowly, weights its three components equally. Internet usage — misses older and rural populations. Life expectancy — influenced by healthcare access but not a perfect proxy for wealth. Uses examples (Switzerland HDI 0.969 vs Niger 0.419) to show how multiple indicators give a fuller picture than any single one.
Secure: Three indicators evaluated with limitations.
Developing: Two indicators with partial limitations.
Emerging: Lists indicators without evaluation.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
“The traditional ‘developed/developing’ binary is no longer useful for understanding the world.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• discuss why the binary is criticised
• discuss the AC, EDC and LIDC alternative
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument. Critique — the binary collapses very different countries into one category (China alongside Mozambique); ignores rapid change since 1990; politically loaded. AC/EDC/LIDC alternative — recognises rising EDCs (China 18% of global GDP, India fifth-largest economy); separates them from LIDCs concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa; tracks change over time. Acknowledges that any classification is imperfect — even AC/EDC/LIDC has fuzzy borders and political risks. Conclusion explicitly weighs whether the new categories solve more problems than they create.
Secure: Both sides considered with named examples; conclusion follows the argument.
Developing: One-sided argument; conclusion present but weak.
Emerging: Generic; few facts; no clear judgement.
[8 marks plus 3 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes bilateral aid?
A) Aid given through international organisations like the World Bank
B) Aid given directly from one government to another
C) Aid donated by charities such as Oxfam
D) Aid sent in the immediate aftermath of a disaster
practice_questions.marks: B) Aid given directly from one government to another [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two types of aid that an LIDC might receive.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each correct type, up to two marks. Acceptable answers include:
• Bilateral aid (government-to-government)
• Multilateral aid (through bodies like the World Bank or UN)
• Emergency / short-term aid
• Long-term development aid
• NGO / charity aid
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how patterns of global trade can hold back development in LIDCs.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear description with two distinct trade patterns linked precisely to held-back development. May include LIDCs exporting low-value primary commodities while importing higher-value manufactured goods, and the impact of unstable world prices.
Secure: Clear description of one or two trade patterns with relevant examples (e.g. coffee, cocoa, copper) linked to development.
Developing: Some description of trade and development with limited link between the two.
Emerging: Simple statement that trade is unfair, with no clear link to development.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how colonialism has contributed to uneven development in the world today.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained explanation linking colonial actions (resource extraction, arbitrary borders, slave trade, lack of investment in local industry) to present-day patterns such as low GNI per capita, weak manufacturing or political instability in former colonies. Specific named examples (e.g. British, French or Belgian colonies in Africa).
Secure: Clear explanation linking two or more colonial impacts to current development with at least one example.
Developing: Some link between colonialism and modern development; explanation may be limited or only one factor used.
Emerging: Simple statement that colonialism caused inequality with no developed reasoning.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why having valuable natural resources does not always lead to development.
Use one example to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated explanation of the resource curse with named country example (e.g. Democratic Republic of Congo and cobalt, or oil-rich states with low HDI). Links resources to weak governance, profit flowing to elites or transnational corporations, conflict over mining areas, and limited reinvestment.
Secure: Clear explanation of two or more reasons (governance, conflict, unequal profit distribution) with a relevant example.
Developing: Limited explanation, perhaps one reason or one example, with some uncertainty about how resources fail to drive development.
Emerging: Simple point that resources do not always help, with no clear reasoning or example.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Aid does more harm than good for low-income developing countries.'
Discuss this view.
Use evidence to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained discussion weighing arguments on both sides with specific evidence. Arguments in support: tied aid forces purchases from donor countries, large loans create debt burdens, free imports can undercut local farmers, corruption can divert funds, long-term aid dependency slows local industry. Arguments against: vaccines and emergency relief save lives (Gavi 17m+ deaths prevented), schools and clinics built (UK aid in Sierra Leone), small-scale NGO projects empower communities, multilateral aid funds infrastructure. Reaches a justified conclusion taking aid type and use into account.
Secure: Clear two-sided discussion with at least one named example on each side and a reasoned conclusion.
Developing: Some discussion of advantages and disadvantages but evidence may be limited and conclusion may not be fully justified.
Emerging: One-sided discussion with little evidence and no clear conclusion.
[8 marks plus 3 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following has the highest life expectancy in the UK?
A) Glasgow
B) Westminster
C) Blackpool
D) Middlesbrough
practice_questions.marks: B) Westminster [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two indicators used to measure development within the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each, max 2:
• Average income / median wage
• Life expectancy
• Employment rate / unemployment rate
• Educational attainment
• Ethnicity
• Broadband access
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two patterns of regional inequality in the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per developed point, max 4:
• Income (1) — London median full-time wages of around £44,000 versus North East at around £29,000 (2 — developed).
• Life expectancy (1) — men in Westminster live around 9 years longer than men in Blackpool (2 — developed).
• Employment (1) — South East unemployment around 3-4% versus parts of the North East exceeding 6% (2 — developed).
• Ethnic diversity (1) — London is 46% non-White compared with rural areas being more than 95% White (2 — developed).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe and explain how deindustrialisation has contributed to uneven development in the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Defines deindustrialisation; identifies regions hit (North East coalfields, Glasgow shipyards, Sheffield steel, South Wales mining) and explains the chain of effects — job losses, lower household income, lower tax revenue, fewer services, depopulation. Replacement industries narrower (e.g. Nissan Sunderland 6,000 jobs versus about 250,000 UK mining jobs in the mid-1970s) leaving structural gaps.
Secure: Process described with named regions and clear cause-effect chain.
Developing: Process partial; one or two regions named; effects implicit.
Emerging: Generic statements about industry closing; no specific evidence.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how location, infrastructure and policy have together reinforced UK regional inequality.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Connects three factors with named UK evidence. Location — South East proximity to London and Europe gives market access; remote rural Wales lacks this. Infrastructure — transport investment per head is much higher in London (Crossrail) than in the North; broadband gaps remain in rural Scotland. Policy — capital spending and headquarters cluster in the South East; recent levelling-up policy attempts to reverse but with limited results so far. Each factor reinforces the others — companies follow infrastructure, infrastructure follows policy, and skilled workers follow companies.
Secure: All three factors discussed with at least one named example; some interaction shown.
Developing: One or two factors covered; interaction implicit.
Emerging: Lists factors without explanation or evidence.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
“Government policy is the most important cause of uneven development in the UK.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• discuss the role of government policy
• discuss alternative causes (location, economic change, infrastructure)
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced evaluation. Policy — targeted spending on London (Crossrail, City), regional aid programmes, levelling-up funding; effects measurable. Alternative causes — geography (proximity to Europe), economic change (deindustrialisation), infrastructure decisions, agglomeration effects (companies cluster where workers cluster). Uses UK evidence (income gaps, life expectancy figures, levelling-up funding totals). Conclusion explicitly weighs whether policy can override location and history, or merely reinforces them.
Secure: Both sides considered with named UK examples; conclusion follows the argument.
Developing: One-sided argument; conclusion present but weakly justified.
Emerging: Generic comments; little UK evidence; no clear judgement.
[8 marks plus 3 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is Nigeria's main export?
A) Cocoa
B) Crude oil
C) Cars
D) Wheat
practice_questions.marks: B) Crude oil [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two named transnational corporations operating in Nigeria.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each correctly named TNC, up to two marks. Acceptable answers include:
• Shell
• ExxonMobil
• Chevron
• MTN
• Dangote
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the relative importance of trade in Nigeria's economic development.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear description of how trade dominates the economy, with crude oil providing roughly 80% of export earnings and most government revenue. Recognises imports include manufactured goods such as machinery and refined fuel.
Secure: Clear description of trade with at least one named export and one named import.
Developing: Some description of trade but limited use of figures or examples.
Emerging: Simple statement that Nigeria trades, with no clear reasoning.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how social factors, such as education and healthcare, affect Nigeria's economic development.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained explanation linking education and healthcare to development. May include rising primary enrolment over 60% but more than 10 million children still out of school; life expectancy around 55 years; how poor health and low literacy reduce productivity. Connects social factors to growth in sectors like fintech where skilled workers are needed.
Secure: Clear explanation of two social factors with relevant figures or named examples.
Developing: Some explanation but with limited link between social factors and economic growth.
Emerging: Simple point that schools and hospitals matter, with no developed reasoning.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain how international investment has shaped Nigeria's recent economic development.
Use named examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated explanation using two or more named investments and showing both benefits and drawbacks. May include oil TNCs (Shell, ExxonMobil, Chevron) creating jobs and tax revenue but causing environmental damage in the Niger Delta; MTN providing mobile networks; Chinese investment in railways, power stations and Lekki deep-sea port. Recognises that profits can flow overseas.
Secure: Clear explanation of two named investments with at least one benefit and one drawback.
Developing: Limited explanation, perhaps one named example, with some uncertainty about long-term impact.
Emerging: Simple statement about foreign companies in Nigeria, with no specific examples.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Nigeria has reached the take-off stage of Rostow's model of economic development.'
Discuss this view.
Use evidence from your case study to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained discussion using specific evidence on both sides and reaching a justified conclusion. Arguments in support: oil, telecoms and fintech sectors growing fast; new infrastructure such as Lekki deep-sea port and railways; urban middle class in Lagos and Abuja; over 200 million mobile connections. Arguments against: rural north remains heavily agricultural and poorer; Boko Haram insurgency holds back development; over-reliance on a single export; high inequality and youth unemployment; Rostow's model itself has been criticised for ignoring colonial history and global inequality.
Secure: Clear two-sided discussion with named evidence and a reasoned conclusion.
Developing: Some discussion but evidence may be limited and conclusion may not be fully justified.
Emerging: One-sided argument with little evidence.
[8 marks plus 3 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the current UK population pyramid?
A) Wide base and narrow top (Stage 1)
B) Narrowing base, growing top (Stage 4)
C) Wide top and narrow base (Stage 5 decline)
D) Identical width at every age
practice_questions.marks: B) Narrowing base, growing top (Stage 4) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two reasons why the UK population is ageing.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each, max 2:
• Improvements in healthcare
• Better nutrition and lifestyle
• Falling birth rate
• Pensions and welfare allowing longer retirement
• Reduction in deaths from infectious disease
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two consequences of an ageing UK population.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per developed point, max 4:
• Rising pension costs (1) reaching £125 billion in 2023 (2 — developed).
• Increased pressure on the NHS (1) with around 40% of beds occupied by over-65s (2 — developed).
• Rising dependency ratio (1) putting pressure on the working-age tax base (2 — developed).
• Growing care crisis (1) with demand for residential care outstripping supply (2 — developed).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe and explain how the UK government has responded to the ageing population.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies and explains three responses — raising the state pension age (66 today, 67 by 2028), workplace pension auto-enrolment (since 2012), and using migration to top up the labour force (post-2004 EU enlargement, Health and Care visas). Connects each to its purpose: reduce cost, encourage saving, fill workforce gaps.
Secure: Two responses described with explanation.
Developing: Names responses but limited explanation.
Emerging: Lists policies without context.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how 21st-century migration has shaped the UK's economy and society.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies major flows (post-2004 EU enlargement, Polish workers; Health and Care visas; Hong Kong BNO; Ukraine refugees) with named statistics (944,000 net migration in the year to March 2023; 17% NHS doctors trained abroad; 1 million Polish arrivals in a decade). Explains both economic benefits (filling skill gaps in NHS, agriculture, construction; net tax contribution) and social effects (cultural diversity, language and faith change in cities). Acknowledges pressures on housing, schools and integration.
Secure: Multiple flows named with effects on at least two sectors.
Developing: One or two flows described; effects partial.
Emerging: Generic comments about migration; no specific UK examples.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
“The UK's ageing population is its biggest demographic challenge.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• discuss the impacts of an ageing UK population
• consider other demographic challenges (migration, urbanisation, regional inequality)
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced evaluation. Ageing — pension costs (£125 billion 2023), NHS pressure (40% beds), dependency ratio rise. Other demographic challenges — managing record net migration (944,000 in the year to March 2023), housing pressures, ageing rural areas versus young cities, regional inequality (Lesson 5). Compares scale and political urgency. Conclusion explicitly weighs which is most pressing and why.
Secure: Both sides discussed with at least one named challenge each; conclusion follows the argument.
Developing: One-sided argument; conclusion present but weak.
Emerging: Generic; few statistics; no clear judgement.
[8 marks plus 3 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes counter-urbanisation?
A) Movement from rural to urban areas
B) Movement from inner city to suburbs
C) Movement from cities to smaller towns and rural areas
D) Movement from suburbs back to the city centre
practice_questions.marks: C) Movement from cities to smaller towns and rural areas [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two factors that drove UK suburbanisation after 1945.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each, max 2:
• Spread of car ownership
• Public transport expansion (rail and bus)
• Council and private house-building programmes
• Desire for larger homes with gardens
• Better schools in suburbs
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two causes of UK counter-urbanisation.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per developed point, max 4:
• Improved transport infrastructure (1) such as the M25 motorway opening in 1986 enabling longer commutes (2 — developed).
• Rise of home computing and remote working (1) reducing the need to live close to city offices (2 — developed).
• Lower house prices in rural areas (1) attracting families seeking value for money and bigger gardens (2 — developed).
• Quality-of-life preference (1) for quieter villages with less pollution and crime (2 — developed).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe and explain why re-urbanisation has accelerated in UK cities since 2000.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies multiple causes — inner-city regeneration (Salford Quays/MediaCityUK), growth of knowledge-economy jobs in central districts (financial, creative), lifestyle preference for short commutes, conversion of warehouses and mills into apartments, public transport investment (Metrolink). Connects each to the inflow of younger professionals and city-centre population growth.
Secure: Three causes with a UK example each.
Developing: One or two causes; example partial.
Emerging: Lists drivers without explanation.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how your chosen UK city has used regeneration and sustainable strategy to manage urban change.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Uses Manchester (or another named UK city). Regeneration — Salford Quays/MediaCityUK brought BBC and ITV jobs; mill conversion grew city-centre population from 1,000 to 60,000; Metrolink connects regenerated centre to outer districts. Sustainable strategy — clean air plan for buses, taxis and lorries; Bee Network integrated transport; carbon budget to halve city emissions by 2025; affordable housing targets. Links regeneration to challenges (housing affordability, transport, air quality) and shows how strategy responds.
Secure: Two or three regeneration and sustainability examples; clear chain of cause and effect.
Developing: One or two examples; effects partial.
Emerging: Generic comments; no specific UK city evidence.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
“Re-urbanisation has been the most positive trend for UK cities.”
Evaluate this statement using your case study.
In your answer you should:
• discuss the benefits of re-urbanisation
• discuss the costs and pressures it creates
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced evaluation. Benefits — growing city-centre populations (Manchester from 1,000 to 60,000), regenerated dockland (Salford Quays), shorter commutes, vibrant cultural scenes, denser sustainable living. Costs — gentrification displacing lower-income households, rising rents (over 30% increase 2018-2024 in central Manchester), pressure on transport (Metrolink overcrowding), housing affordability, persistent air quality issues. Conclusion explicitly weighs whether re-urbanisation has done more good than harm and for whom.
Secure: Both sides considered with named UK case-study evidence; conclusion follows the argument.
Developing: One-sided argument; conclusion present but weak.
Emerging: Generic; few facts; no clear judgement.
[8 marks plus 3 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following defines a megacity?
A) Any capital city
B) A city with over 1 million people
C) A city with over 10 million people
D) A city where most people work in services
practice_questions.marks: C) A city with over 10 million people [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two pull factors that attract people to Lagos.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each correct pull factor, up to two marks. Acceptable answers include:
• Greater chance of paid work / formal jobs
• Better schools and education
• Better healthcare
• Wider entertainment, culture and family connections
• Tech and creative industries (Nollywood, fintech)
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how the global pattern of megacities has changed since 1950.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear description of the change with figures. May include only New York and Tokyo as megacities in 1950, around 10 by 1990 and over 30 today. Notes the shift from ACs to LIDCs and EDCs, and the rise of Asian and African megacities such as Delhi, Shanghai, Dhaka, Lagos and Kinshasa.
Secure: Clear description of the global shift with at least one named example.
Developing: Some description of growth but limited use of figures or examples.
Emerging: Simple statement that more cities have got bigger.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the social and environmental consequences of rapid urbanisation in an LIDC or EDC city you have studied.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained explanation linking causes of rapid urbanisation in Lagos to clear social and environmental impacts. May include informal settlements like Makoko (around 60% of residents in informal housing), traffic congestion and air pollution from older vehicles, flooding worsened by blocked drains, waste-management pressure at sites such as Olusosun.
Secure: Clear explanation of two consequences (one social, one environmental) with named examples.
Developing: Some explanation but with limited examples or only one type of consequence.
Emerging: Simple list of problems with no clear case study reference.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how migration has shaped the character and ways of life of one major city in an LIDC or EDC.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated explanation using Lagos as case study. Covers internal migration from rural Nigeria (especially the north) and international migration from neighbouring states like Benin, Togo and Ghana. Links migration to multi-ethnic communities (Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa), markets like Balogun and Computer Village, the spread of Afrobeats and Nollywood, and to the divide between high-rise districts like Victoria Island and informal settlements like Makoko.
Secure: Clear explanation of how migration has changed Lagos with at least two named features and one figure.
Developing: Limited explanation, perhaps one named example, with some uncertainty about the link between migration and ways of life.
Emerging: Simple statement that many groups live in Lagos with little supporting detail.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Sustainable strategies have successfully tackled the challenges facing Lagos.'
Discuss this view.
Use evidence from your case study.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained discussion weighing strategies on both sides with specific evidence and a justified conclusion. Arguments in support: Bus Rapid Transit lanes move commuters faster than cars; Blue Line metro (opened 2023) cuts journeys from over an hour to about 20 minutes; Lekki deep-sea port spreads economic activity east; Eko Atlantic reclaims flood-resilient land. Arguments against: housing shortages and informal settlements such as Makoko continue; traffic and pollution remain severe; Eko Atlantic is criticised for being for the wealthy; flooding still affects many districts; the gap between rich and poor is widening.
Secure: Clear two-sided discussion with named strategies and a reasoned conclusion.
Developing: Some discussion but evidence may be limited and conclusion may not be fully justified.
Emerging: One-sided discussion with little evidence.
[8 marks plus 3 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following air masses brings warm and wet weather to the UK?
A) Polar continental
B) Tropical maritime
C) Arctic maritime
D) Tropical continental
practice_questions.marks: B) Tropical maritime [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two reasons why the UK has a milder climate than other countries at the same latitude.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each, max 2:
• The North Atlantic Drift brings warm water past UK shores
• Prevailing south-westerly winds bring tropical maritime air
• The UK is surrounded by the sea (no extreme continentality)
• The Gulf Stream warms the air over coastal regions
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two effects of an extreme weather event you have studied in the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per developed point, max 4:
• Storm Desmond (2015) flooded 5,200 homes in Cumbria (1) including Carlisle, Keswick and Cockermouth (2 — developed).
• Total economic damage exceeded £500 million (1), with insurance payouts of similar scale and weeks of school and business closures (2 — developed).
• Environmental effects included new river channels and landslides on Lake District fells (1) and pollution of Lake Bassenthwaite by farm chemicals (2 — developed).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe and explain how an extreme weather event in your UK case study affected people and the environment.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Names the event (Storm Desmond, December 2015) with rainfall figure (341.4 mm in 24 hours). Identifies social effects (5,200 homes flooded, 46,000 power cuts, three deaths, schools and railway closed for weeks). Identifies environmental effects (new river channels, landslides, lake pollution). Connects causes to consequences with locational specificity.
Secure: Names the event with at least one social and one environmental effect.
Developing: Effects described but partially specific.
Emerging: Generic effects with no named UK event.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how climate change is making extreme weather more frequent in the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Uses Met Office data (10 hottest years on record since 2002, heavy rainfall up 4% per decade since 1961, July 2022 heatwave 10 times more likely due to climate change). Links warming to atmospheric water-holding capacity, jet stream shifts and intensified storms. Provides specific UK examples (2022 heatwave, Storm Eunice 122 mph, Storm Desmond rainfall record). Acknowledges natural variability while showing the climate change signal.
Secure: Multiple events linked with statistics; cause-effect chain present.
Developing: Names events without statistics, or links partially.
Emerging: Generic; no UK statistics.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
“Hard engineering is the most effective way to manage UK flood risk.”
Evaluate this statement using your case study.
In your answer you should:
• discuss the benefits of hard engineering
• discuss alternatives such as natural flood management
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument. Hard engineering benefits — Carlisle Flood Defence Scheme upgraded with higher walls and pumps protects city of 75,000; sea walls protect coastal towns. Drawbacks — high cost, can shift problems downstream, requires constant maintenance. Alternatives — Stockdalewath natural flood management uses leaky dams and tree planting to slow flow; Medmerry-style managed retreat. Conclusion explicitly weighs cost-effectiveness, sustainability and community trust before reaching a judgement.
Secure: Both sides considered with named UK examples; conclusion follows the argument.
Developing: One-sided argument; conclusion present but weak.
Emerging: Generic; few facts; no clear judgement.
[8 marks plus 3 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a natural cause of climate change?
A) Burning of coal in power stations
B) Deforestation in the Amazon
C) Variations in the Earth's orbit (Milankovitch cycles)
D) Cattle farming
practice_questions.marks: C) Variations in the Earth's orbit (Milankovitch cycles) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two sources of evidence used to study past climate change.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each correct source, up to two marks. Acceptable answers include:
• Ice cores
• Tree rings (dendrochronology)
• Global temperature records / instrumental records
• Paintings and diaries
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how ice cores are used as evidence of past climate change.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear description of the process. May include drilling deep into ice sheets in Antarctica or Greenland; layers of compacted snow trap air bubbles; analysing those bubbles gives carbon dioxide concentrations; oxygen isotopes give past temperatures; record reaches back over 800,000 years.
Secure: Clear description of two stages of the method with at least one figure or named ice sheet.
Developing: Some description but limited link to climate evidence.
Emerging: Simple statement that scientists drill ice with no clear method.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how human activities have contributed to the enhanced greenhouse effect.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained explanation linking specific human activities to higher greenhouse-gas concentrations and warming. May include burning fossil fuels in power stations and vehicles releasing carbon dioxide; deforestation reducing carbon absorption; methane from cattle farming and rice paddies; CO2 rising from around 280 ppm in 1850 to over 420 ppm today; link to about 1.1°C global warming.
Secure: Clear explanation of two human activities with figures and link to warming.
Developing: Some explanation of human activities but limited link to the greenhouse effect.
Emerging: Simple statement that humans cause warming with no developed reasoning.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain how natural causes can also contribute to changes in the Earth's climate.
Use named examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated explanation of two or more natural causes with named examples. Solar output (Maunder Minimum 1645–1715 linked to Little Ice Age cooling); Milankovitch cycles pacing long ice ages; volcanic activity (Mount Pinatubo 1991 cooling global temperatures by around 0.5°C). Recognises that natural causes operate on different time scales from current human-driven change.
Secure: Clear explanation of two natural causes with at least one named example.
Developing: Limited explanation, perhaps one natural cause, with some uncertainty about its impact.
Emerging: Simple list of natural causes with no examples.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Modern climate change is mostly the result of human activity rather than natural cycles.'
Discuss this view.
Use evidence to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained discussion weighing evidence on both sides and reaching a justified conclusion. Arguments in support: CO2 levels rising from 280 ppm to over 420 ppm; rate of change far faster than past natural cycles; ice-core record over 800,000 years shows no comparable spike; warming closely tracks the rise in fossil-fuel use since the Industrial Revolution; about 1.1°C of warming since 1850; Arctic sea-ice loss roughly 40% since the 1980s. Arguments referencing natural variability: orbital cycles, solar output (Maunder Minimum) and volcanic eruptions have caused past changes; some natural variability still occurs alongside human warming. Reaches a justified conclusion that human activity is the dominant driver of recent rapid change.
Secure: Clear two-sided discussion with named evidence and a reasoned conclusion.
Developing: Some discussion but evidence may be limited and conclusion may not be fully justified.
Emerging: One-sided argument with little evidence.
[8 marks plus 3 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the UK's largest onshore wind farm?
A) Hornsea Two
B) Whitelee
C) Preston New Road
D) Drax
practice_questions.marks: B) Whitelee [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two ways UK humans modify ecosystems to provide energy.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each, max 2:
• Wind farms (onshore or offshore)
• Fracking for shale gas
• Hydroelectric schemes (e.g. Cruachan, Dinorwig)
• Solar farms
• Coal and gas-fired power stations
• Nuclear power stations
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two effects of mechanised farming on UK ecosystems.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per developed point, max 4:
• Hedgerow loss (1) reduces habitat for birds, mammals and pollinators (2 — developed).
• Use of fertilisers and pesticides (1) leads to nitrate run-off polluting UK rivers and reservoirs (2 — developed).
• Soil thinning from intensive cultivation (1) reduces fertility and increases flood risk through faster run-off (2 — developed).
• Pollinator decline (1) with UK pollinator populations halved since 1980 (2 — developed).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe and explain how wind farms have changed the UK's energy mix.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies wind generates around 30% of UK electricity in 2024 (up from below 1% in 2000). Explains both onshore (Whitelee, 215 turbines) and offshore (Hornsea Two, 1.32 GW, 1.4 million homes). Connects growth to government renewable subsidies, low operating costs and net-zero targets. Recognises trade-offs: visual impact in uplands, seabed disturbance during installation.
Secure: Identifies wind contribution with one named UK example.
Developing: Lists wind farms without context.
Emerging: Generic comments about wind energy.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how reservoirs and water transfer schemes change UK ecosystems.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Uses named UK examples. Reservoirs — Kielder Water (200 billion litres, supplies the North East), Haweswater and Thirlmere (Manchester pipeline since 19th century) flooded valleys, displaced communities, altered downstream river flow. Transfer schemes — Ely Ouse-Essex transfer moves water from Norfolk to Essex, raises questions about whose ecosystem loses and whose gains. Acknowledges sustainability case (drier southern summers under climate change) alongside ecological cost.
Secure: Two named examples; clear chain of cause and effect.
Developing: One example with partial explanation.
Emerging: Generic; no UK examples.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
“The benefits of modifying UK ecosystems outweigh the environmental costs.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• discuss the benefits of UK ecosystem modification
• discuss environmental costs
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument with named UK examples. Benefits — food security (60% UK food produced domestically), energy supply (wind 30% of electricity), water security (Kielder Water supplies the North East). Costs — biodiversity loss (pollinators halved), seabed damage from trawling and offshore wind installation, fracking earthquakes (Preston New Road), drowned valleys (Haweswater), reduced river flow downstream of reservoirs. Conclusion explicitly weighs whether benefits are sustainable in the long term.
Secure: Both sides considered with named UK examples; conclusion follows the argument.
Developing: One-sided argument; conclusion present but weak.
Emerging: Generic; few facts; no clear judgement.
[8 marks plus 3 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the minimum sea-surface temperature needed for a tropical storm to form?
A) 18°C
B) 22°C
C) 27°C
D) 32°C
practice_questions.marks: C) 27°C [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify the three atmospheric circulation cells found in each hemisphere.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks for naming all three correctly: Hadley cell, Ferrel cell and Polar cell. Award one mark for two correct.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the global distribution of tropical storms.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear description with named locations and latitude band. May include concentration around 5–30° north and south of the equator; main areas the Atlantic, West Pacific, Bay of Bengal and around northern Australia; absent from the equator itself and from cooler ocean basins.
Secure: Clear description of distribution with at least one named area and reference to latitude.
Developing: Some description of distribution with limited reference to specific places.
Emerging: Simple statement that storms are tropical with no detail.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the global atmospheric circulation creates the world's hot deserts.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained explanation linking the Hadley cell to deserts. May include warm moist air rising at the equator, releasing rain over rainforests, drifting polewards as drier air aloft, sinking at around 30° latitude, warming by compression, suppressing cloud and rainfall. Names major deserts (Sahara, Arabian, Kalahari, Australian Outback, south-west USA).
Secure: Clear explanation of two stages with at least one named desert.
Developing: Some explanation but limited link between the cell and deserts.
Emerging: Simple statement that deserts are dry, with no clear cause.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain the conditions and processes that lead to the formation of a tropical storm.
Use named examples or features in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated explanation that names the four conditions (sea-surface temperature ≥27°C; about 70m of warm water; low wind shear; 5–30° from the equator) and links them to processes. Describes warm moist air rising, water vapour condensing and releasing energy, air spiralling inwards under the Coriolis effect, formation of the eye and eyewall.
Secure: Clear explanation of three conditions with at least one process linked correctly.
Developing: Limited explanation, perhaps one or two conditions with weak link to formation.
Emerging: Simple list of conditions with no process explanation.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Climate change is making tropical storms more dangerous.'
Discuss this view.
Use evidence to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained discussion separating frequency from intensity, with specific evidence and a justified conclusion. Arguments in support: warmer sea-surface temperatures fuel stronger storms; more Category 4 and 5 storms in recent decades; storms are dumping more rainfall and producing larger storm surges; rising sea levels worsen coastal flooding. Arguments against: total number of named storms each year (around 80–90 globally) has not clearly risen; some basins show year-to-year variability rather than long-term trends; better warning and evacuation save more lives than in the past. Reaches a justified conclusion that storms are becoming more dangerous in intensity and impact, even if not in number.
Secure: Clear two-sided discussion with named evidence and a reasoned conclusion.
Developing: Some discussion but evidence may be limited and conclusion may not be fully justified.
Emerging: One-sided argument with little evidence.
[8 marks plus 3 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes El Nino?
A) A cool phase of the Pacific Ocean linked to flooding in Australia
B) A warm phase of the Pacific Ocean linked to drought in Australia
C) A storm system in the Indian Ocean
D) A type of monsoon over India
practice_questions.marks: B) A warm phase of the Pacific Ocean linked to drought in Australia [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two ways that Australians adapted to the Millennium Drought.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each correct adaptation, up to two marks. Acceptable answers include:
• Building desalination plants in Sydney, Perth, Melbourne or Adelaide
• Domestic water restrictions / hosepipe bans
• Rainwater tanks and greywater reuse
• Drip irrigation and drought-tolerant crops
• Murray-Darling Basin Plan (2012)
• Improved ENSO forecasting from the Bureau of Meteorology
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how the trade winds change during an El Nino event.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear description that in normal years strong trade winds blow east-to-west, pushing warm water towards Australia and Indonesia, and that during El Nino these winds weaken or reverse, allowing the warm pool of water to slosh back east, taking rainfall with it.
Secure: Clear description of the change in trade winds with at least one location named.
Developing: Some description but limited link between wind change and rainfall pattern.
Emerging: Simple statement that winds change.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how El Nino events can lead to drought in Australia.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained explanation linking weakened trade winds to warmer water in the central/eastern Pacific, rainfall shifting east towards South America, and dry conditions over Australia. Notes the link to higher fire risk and falling reservoir levels. May include reference to the Millennium Drought 2001–2009 or 2015–16 El Nino as supporting examples.
Secure: Clear explanation of two stages with at least one named example.
Developing: Some explanation but limited link between Pacific changes and Australian rainfall.
Emerging: Simple statement that El Nino causes drought.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain the effects of one drought event on people and the environment.
Use a named case study in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated explanation using the Millennium Drought (2001–2009) with named effects on both people and the environment. People: wheat harvests fell 36% in 2002; livestock losses; reservoir levels below 30%; water restrictions; rural mental-health crisis and migration. Environment: Murray-Darling lower reaches failed to reach the sea; wetlands shrank; river red gum die-off; Black Saturday bushfires February 2009 (173 deaths); 2009 Sydney dust storm.
Secure: Clear explanation of two human and one environmental effect with named figures.
Developing: Limited explanation, perhaps one type of effect or weak case study detail.
Emerging: Simple list of impacts with no named figures.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Adaptation has successfully reduced the impact of drought in your case study area.'
Discuss this view.
Use evidence from the case study you have studied.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained discussion with named adaptations on both sides and a justified conclusion. Arguments in support: large desalination plants in Sydney, Perth, Melbourne and Adelaide give drought-proof city water; permanent water-saving rules and rainwater tanks have cut household demand; drought-tolerant wheat and drip irrigation reduce farm losses; the Murray-Darling Basin Plan (2012) sets caps on river extractions; better ENSO forecasting allows planning ahead. Arguments against: desalination is energy-hungry and expensive; the Basin Plan has been weakened by political lobbying; many smaller farms still went out of business; recent El Nino events of 2018–19 still caused major stress; long-term climate projections show drying continues. Reaches a justified conclusion that Australia is more resilient but not drought-proof.
Secure: Clear two-sided discussion with named adaptations and a reasoned conclusion.
Developing: Some discussion but limited evidence and unjustified conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided argument with little evidence.
[8 marks plus 3 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a renewable energy source in the UK?
A) Natural gas
B) Coal
C) Wind
D) Diesel oil
practice_questions.marks: C) Wind [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two UK renewable electricity sources.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each, max 2:
• Wind (onshore or offshore)
• Solar / photovoltaic
• Hydroelectric
• Biomass
• Tidal / wave
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways the UK has changed its energy mix since 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per developed point, max 4:
• Coal has been phased out (1) from 67% of electricity in 1990 to effectively zero in 2024 with Ratcliffe-on-Soar's closure (2 — developed).
• Wind has grown rapidly (1) from below 1% of electricity in 2000 to around 30% in 2024 (2 — developed).
• Solar has scaled (1) to around 5% of UK electricity, with continued growth in domestic and farm-scale installations (2 — developed).
• Nuclear has been refreshed (1) with new stations at Hinkley Point C and Sizewell C planned to replace ageing reactors (2 — developed).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe and explain the role of offshore wind in the UK's renewable transition.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies offshore wind as a major renewable source, scaling rapidly. Explains UK advantages (shallow North Sea, consistent winds, public acceptance compared to onshore). Names projects (Hornsea Two 1.32 GW; Dogger Bank 3.6 GW under construction; total UK offshore capacity already over 14 GW). Connects to net zero strategy and falling costs.
Secure: Identifies offshore wind with one named UK project and rough capacity.
Developing: General comments about wind without UK specificity.
Emerging: Lists wind as renewable; no detail.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the UK is managing the transition to a sustainable energy system.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies three pillars: scaling renewables (Hornsea, Dogger Bank, solar growth), upgrading the grid (HVDC interconnectors, storage), and reducing demand (insulation, heat pumps, EVs, 2030 petrol and diesel car ban). Uses named projects with capacity figures and policy targets. Acknowledges trade-offs (cost, intermittency, public acceptance) and connects to the legal net-zero-by-2050 target.
Secure: Two pillars discussed with named UK examples.
Developing: One pillar covered; others implicit.
Emerging: Generic; no UK projects.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
“The UK should rely entirely on renewable energy by 2050.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• discuss the case for full renewable reliance
• discuss the role of nuclear and gas
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument. Case for renewables — net-zero target, falling costs, scale (Hornsea, Dogger Bank), Orkney already net-positive renewable. Counter-case — intermittency requires baseload (nuclear at about 12%), gas remains flexible (about 27%), grid still being upgraded, security against imports of materials and electricity. Conclusion explicitly weighs whether 2050 is realistic and what mix is most resilient. Specific UK examples used throughout.
Secure: Both sides considered with named UK examples; conclusion follows the argument.
Developing: One-sided argument; conclusion present but weak.
Emerging: Generic; few facts; no clear judgement.
[8 marks plus 3 SPaG]
